newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai authorities win first round in finance battle.
newsitem.headline: Thai authorities win first round in finance battle.

text.p: If Thailand's three-month-old coalition government has one feather in its cap, it must be for averting the Mexico-style financial meltdown that so many feared was on its way last week.

Thanks to a package of measures, including plans to rescue troubled property developers and their financiers through a multi-billion-dollar bond issue, confidence in the country's financial health and economy has started to creep back.
But analysts said on Wednesday that the steps did little more than paper over cracks in the financial system and could inhibit a natural shake-out of the property market.

"This is a welcome strategy, it's part of the government's overall effort to really prevent a failure in finance companies and banks," said Desmond Supple, chief economist for Asia Pacific at BZW Singapore.
"So it is a welcome policy measure, but it should not be seen as a solution to the problem, rather postponing an inevitable restructuring of the financial sector," he said.

Last week, the government ordered 10 finance companies to raise capital and toughened loan-loss reserve requirements for the country's 15 banks and 91 finance firms, many of which have crippling exposure to the bloated property market.

On Tuesday the cabinet approved plans to issue up to 100 billion baht ($3.87 billion) in zero-coupon bonds, proceeds of which would refinance troubled property projects and inject liquidity into cash-strapped finance firms.
The stock market, which has lost about half of its value in the past year, celebrated the "property bond" with gains in three sessions in a row. But analysts remain sceptical.

"The cabinet has only approved it in principle," said one analyst at a Thai securities and finance house. "Here in Thailand one scheme after another is proposed, bandied about and then left in the dustbin. There's no guarantee that won't happen again."

He said the scheme, assuming it is implemented, would probably fail to deal with the enormity of the debt problem facing the financial sector. "It's papering over a crack that's turning into a canyon," he said.

Analysts believe that as much as 10 percent of bank and finance firm loans could be classified as doubtful or sub-standard assets. Many draw comparisons with Japan, where reform of the financial system has been slow and banks persistently underestimate the weight of bad loans.

Graham Catterwell, head of equities at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, believes that by forcing finance firms to raise capital and make more provisions for bad debt the government is making the institutions pay for their own reckless lending.
Some analysts say the authorities' other steps may skew market forces, which would otherwise have allowed property prices to find their own level and probably sent many finance houses to the wall.
"Market forces aren't being allowed to reprise and punish as they should," said the securities and finance house analyst.
He argued that the ideal world solution would be for finance firms to weather the storm, keeping fingers crossed that better economic fortunes would eventually solve their problems.
Giving free rein to market forces is not something that has come naturally to Thailand's succession of governments.
The Bank of Thailand is thought to have spent billions of dollars in recent weeks to quash speculation against the baht, which it insists will not be devalued.
That determination has kept interest rates high, which have done nothing to alleviate the finance sector's problems or the country's alarming current account deficit.
